As Kanye West whipped the crowd into a frenzy with hits such as "Gold Digger" and "Through the Wire," his mom waved her hands in the air side to side and bobbed to the beats. When asked if her son would sell more records than 50 Cent (both rappers released their albums on September 11), she answered coyly. "Good music will win out," she said with a smile and a wink. (Her son's label is named Good Music.)  Gallery: Donda and Kanye » . Kanye frequently mentioned Donda in his lyrics. He wrote about her determination that he earn a college degree, as well as the steadfast encouragement she gave him after he chose to build a career in rap. Donda, who died over the weekend at age 58, came across as both deeply affectionate and strong-willed.

In “Can’t Tell Me Nothing,” from his then-newest album, “Graduation,” Kanye describes his mother trying to talk him out of buying expensive jewelry and Louis Vuitton products. In “Touch the Sky,” a song on his 2005 release “Late Registration,” he remembers Donda driving him in a U-Haul van from Chicago, Illinois, to New York.

That album also included “Hey Mama,” which she inspired. In the song, Kanye expresses how proud he is of her, acknowledges that he sometimes behaves foolishly, promises to return to school, thanks her for the opportunities she gave him and says he wants to make her proud.

Donda clearly took pride in her son as well. She frequently went to his concerts, where she could often be seen dancing and rapping along to the cleaner lyrics that received radio play.

At the MTV Video Music Awards in September, Donda and a group of female friends sat in the VIP area during a Rolling Stone magazine party. While Kanye energized the audience with songs including “Gold Digger” and “Through the Wire,” she moved to the music, waving her hands from side to side and nodding with the rhythm.

Asked whether Kanye would outsell 50 Cent—both artists released albums on September 11—Donda responded playfully that good music would ultimately prevail, smiling and winking as she spoke. The remark also referenced her son’s record label, Good Music.

“Graduation” later decisively outsold 50 Cent’s “Curtis.” Kanye’s album entered the Billboard chart at No. 1 and moved more than 950,000 copies during its first week.

Before Kanye achieved worldwide fame, Donda taught English at Chicago State University. In 2004, she left her role as chair of the school’s English department so she could manage her son’s rapidly growing career full time.

Mother and son later worked together on “Raising Kanye: Life Lessons From the Mother of a Hip Hop Star,” published in May. More recently, Donda became chief executive of Super Good, the parent organization of Kanye West Enterprises. She also chaired the Kanye West Foundation, whose mission—appropriately, given her emphasis on education—was to prevent students from leaving school before graduating.

**Kanye West’s Music Traced a Lifelong Bond With His Mother**

Long before Kanye West renamed himself Ye and became as famous for controversy as for music, his songs repeatedly returned to one central figure: his mother, Donda West.

A scholar and former English professor, Donda raised West largely on her own in Chicago after divorcing his father. She supported his ambitions when he left college to pursue music, later managing his career and leading the foundation that bore her name. In West’s early work, she became both a character and a moral reference point — the person whose sacrifice gave meaning to his success.

That relationship was expressed most directly in “Hey Mama,” released on his 2005 album, *Late Registration*, though West had performed versions of the song years earlier. Built around memories of financial struggle, childhood loyalty and his mother’s encouragement, the track presents fame not simply as personal triumph but as repayment. West recalls Donda working to provide for him and promises to give her the life she deserved.

Its warmth set the song apart from the bravado that often defined his public persona. When West performed “Hey Mama” with Donda present, it functioned as a public thank-you — an unusually unguarded portrait of a son who saw his mother as his earliest believer.

The bond also surfaced in “Touch the Sky,” another *Late Registration* track. The song is primarily a celebration of ambition and escape, following West from a struggling producer to a star. But within that rise, he frames success partly through his mother’s pride. The reference is brief compared with “Hey Mama,” yet revealing: reaching the top mattered because she had witnessed the uncertainty that came before it.

By 2007’s “Can’t Tell Me Nothing,” West’s music had grown more conflicted. The song is not a tribute to Donda, but its themes — money, arrogance, guilt and self-discipline — illuminate the tension between the values associated with his mother and the temptations of celebrity. West depicts himself as successful enough to reject advice, yet self-aware enough to know that wealth has not delivered wisdom. The track’s defiance carries an undercurrent of accountability, as if the voice that once guided him remains present even when he resists it.

Donda West died in November 2007, months after the release of *Graduation*, which included “Can’t Tell Me Nothing.” Her death transformed the emotional context of her son’s catalog. Performances of “Hey Mama” became acts of mourning, and West’s later music increasingly explored grief, isolation, faith and the instability of fame.

He would continue to place her at the center of his artistic identity, naming his creative company DONDA and two later albums, *Donda* and *Donda 2*, after her. Across those projects and his earlier songs, she appears not only as a parent but as a symbol of home, belief and moral grounding.

Taken together, “Hey Mama,” “Touch the Sky” and “Can’t Tell Me Nothing” chart different sides of that relationship: gratitude, shared aspiration and the struggle between guidance and self-will. They also show how West’s bond with his mother helped shape the emotional architecture of his music — before her death and long after it.

# Donda West, mother and mentor of Kanye West, dies at 58

**LOS ANGELES (CNN) —** Donda West, the mother, longtime manager and guiding influence of rapper Kanye West, died Saturday in Los Angeles. She was 58.

West’s relationship with her son extended far beyond that of a parent and child. A former university professor and academic administrator, she helped shape his ambitions, supported his early pursuit of music and later became a central figure in his business and philanthropic work.

Kanye West frequently credited his mother with giving him the confidence to pursue a career in hip-hop. Their close bond was reflected in his music, most notably in “Hey Mama,” a tribute released on his 2005 album, *Late Registration*.

Earlier in 2007, Donda West published *Raising Kanye: Life Lessons from the Mother of a Hip-Hop Superstar*. The book recounted her son’s childhood and rise to fame while presenting lessons about parenting, education and encouraging a child’s creativity.

After leaving academia, West became involved in her son’s career and business ventures. She served as chief executive of West Brands and chaired the Kanye West Foundation, an organization created to support educational programs and address dropout rates.

Her public role alongside her son continued into the final months of her life. In September 2007, she accompanied him to the MTV Video Music Awards in Las Vegas, where he performed and received multiple nominations.

Donda West had previously led the English department at Chicago State University and spent decades in higher education before retiring to work with her son full time.

She died one day after undergoing cosmetic surgery. The Los Angeles County coroner later said she died from heart disease while experiencing multiple postoperative factors following liposuction and breast-reduction procedures, and that no single factor could be identified as the sole cause.

Her death came as Kanye West was enjoying enormous commercial success with his third album, *Graduation*. For the artist, however, the loss was deeply personal: Donda West had been not only his mother, but also his teacher, advocate, manager and most visible supporter.
